title: Human metapneumovirus infection in hospitalized children: a four-year retrospective study from a tertiary pediatric hospital

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is an important viral cause of acute respiratory infections, particularly in young children, and may lead to hospitalization for lower respiratory tract disease. However, detailed clinical data from hospitalized pediatric cohorts remain limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study combined two complementary datasets from a tertiary pediatric hospital in Palermo, Italy. The clinical cohort comprised 78 of the pediatric cases who were hospitalized in the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Unit between January 2022 and May 2025 and had complete clinical records.
analysis.methods: Demographic, clinical, laboratory, radiological, and therapeutic data were collected and analyzed through IBM SPSS Statistics using descriptive statistics and exploratory bivariate analyses. Continuous variables were summarized as median and interquartile range (IQR), while categorical variables were reported as absolute frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between children who received antibiotics and those who did not were performed using Pearson’s chi-square or exact tests, as appropriate.
analysis.main_results: The most frequent signs and symptoms were cough (64;82.1%), fever (59;75.6%), and signs of respiratory distress, including tachypnea (48;61.5%) and subcostal retraction (38;48.7%). Hyporexia (32;41%) and coryza (29;37.2%) were also common. Chest X-ray was performed in 41 (52.6%) patients and showed abnormal findings in all cases, most commonly consolidation patterns. Viral coinfections were detected in 25.6% of patients, and bacterial organisms were detected in 24.4%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Our findings describe the clinical characteristics and management of hospitalized children with hMPV infection in a tertiary pediatric center, highlighting the clinical relevance of hMPV among hospitalized children in our center. Moreover, the high rate of antibiotic prescription observed in this cohort highlights the diagnostic challenges in distinguishing viral from bacterial respiratory infections and underscores the importance of improved antimicrobial stewardship and virological surveillance in pediatric respiratory disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can cautiously inform improved antimicrobial stewardship and virological surveillance in pediatric respiratory disease, emphasizing the need for better diagnostic tools to differentiate viral from bacterial infections in hospitalized children.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias, as it included only 78 hospitalized pediatric cases with complete clinical records. The evidence strength is moderate due to the limited sample size and the focus on a single tertiary pediatric center.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the clinical characteristics and management of hospitalized children with human metapneumovirus (hMPV) infection in a tertiary pediatric hospital in Palermo, Italy, over a four-year period. The research highlights the importance of hMPV as a cause of acute respiratory infections in young children, particularly those requiring hospitalization. The study combined two datasets, one describing the temporal distribution of hMPV infections and the other focusing on clinical data from 78 hospitalized cases. Key findings include the high prevalence of symptoms such as cough, fever, and respiratory distress, as well as the frequent use of antibiotics despite limited bacterial coinfections. The study underscores the diagnostic challenges in differentiating viral from bacterial respiratory infections and calls for improved antimicrobial stewardship and virological surveillance. However, the study is limited by its retrospective design and potential selection bias, as it included only a subset of cases with complete records, which may affect the generalizability of the findings.

title: Emerging Trends in the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management of Human Metapneumovirus-Associated Respiratory Infections

analysis.scope_and_question: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) infection and disease. The review focuses on the pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management of HMPV-associated respiratory infections, particularly in vulnerable populations such as young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on HMPV infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Human metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against HMPV remains unproven. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The virus evades immune responses via multiple mechanisms, contributing to disease severity, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although supportive care is currently the mainstay, emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions. Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections. Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Ongoing research into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines is critical for effective disease management.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) infections, emphasizing its impact on vulnerable populations. The evidence highlights the virus's targeting of respiratory epithelium and the immune responses it triggers. While investigational therapies like fusion and protease inhibitors show promise, their efficacy remains unproven. Vaccine development is ongoing, with several candidates in early stages. The review underscores the need for further clinical trials, improved diagnostics, and public awareness to address the public health burden of HMPV. Despite the lack of specific treatments and vaccines, the study suggests that emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions.

title: Risk classification of severe pneumonia at admission in children with human metapneumovirus infection: development of a machine learning model based on retrospective data from 854 cases

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning model to accurately classify the risk of severe pneumonia in children infected with hMPV, addressing the need for better diagnostic tools in this context.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 854 hospitalized children with hMPV-associated pneumonia at Kunming Children’s Hospital from December 2019 to March 2025, stratifying them into severe and non-severe pneumonia groups.
analysis.methods: The study utilized a machine learning approach, including feature selection with LASSO regression, and compared six models (logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, naïve Bayes, multilayer perceptron, random forest, and XGBoost) on a training set, with model performance evaluated on a testing set using AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score.
analysis.main_results: XGBoost and logistic regression models demonstrated comparable performance, with XGBoost achieving an AUC of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.84–0.90) and 0.78 (95% CI: 0.72–0.85) on the training and testing sets, respectively. SHAP analysis identified wheezing, age, and pulmonary rales as the most influential predictors.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study successfully developed and validated machine learning models, particularly XGBoost and logistic regression, for risk classification of severe pneumonia in children with hMPV infection, demonstrating strong discriminative performance and clinical utility.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The models may serve as a valuable decision-support tool for risk stratification of high-risk pediatric patients with hMPV infection, aiding in clinical decision-making and resource allocation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and the use of a single hospital, which may affect generalizability. The sample size is moderate, and the models were not compared against other established methods.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed and validated machine learning models to classify the risk of severe pneumonia in children with hMPV infection, demonstrating strong performance and potential clinical utility.

title: Epidemiology and lagged climatic drivers of pediatric viral lower respiratory tract infections in Tianjin, China (2023–2025)

analysis.research_question_and_background: (C) Annual case burden, stacked by pathogen.Grouped bar and stacked bar chart panel showing (A) case numbers and percentages for six pathogens, (B) specimen composition by pathogen, and (C) annual case burden from 2023 to 2025.
analysis.study_design_and_population: HRV was the most frequently detected virus (796 cases, 30.7%), followed by ADV (692, 26.6%), RSV (536, 20.6%), HBoV (313, 12.1%), IFV (155, 6.0%) and HMPV (105, 4.0%) (Figure 2A; Table 1).
analysis.methods: Pathogen–climate associations were estimated using a quasi-Poisson model that adjusted for seasonality, secular trend, and lagged meteorological exposures.ResultsAmong 2,597 virus-positive cases, the leading pathogens were HRV (30.7%), ADV (26.6%), and RSV (20.6%), followed by HBoV (12.1%), IFV (6.0%), and HMPV (4.0%).
analysis.main_results: RSV and HBoV were most prevalent in infants and toddlers, in line with airway and immune development (Feng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022); ADV peaked in school-aged children and IFV in the older preschool-to-school-age range, consistent with close-contact transmission in schools and other crowded settings (Fang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023); and HMPV showed an intermediate distribution.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: To our knowledge, the dataset is unusual for northern China in spanning six respiratory viruses, including the comparatively under-surveyed HRV, HBoV and HMPV, over the full 2023–2025 post-pandemic rebound window, with a complete and time-matched monthly meteorological record.4.1Principal epidemiological featuresAcross the six viruses, HRV, ADV and RSV were the leading causes of pediatric LRTI, and each pathogen carried a well-defined demographic profile.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The strong age-group × pathogen association reinforces the need for an explicitly age-stratified surveillance framework.The six pathogens also fell into two distinct seasonal groups.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Co-infection occurred in 4.5% of positives, centered on HRV-containing combinations whose clinical severity remains to be defined.

analysis.summary_en: (C) Annual case burden, stacked by pathogen.Grouped bar and stacked bar chart panel showing (A) case numbers and percentages for six pathogens, (B) specimen composition by pathogen, and (C) annual case burden from 2023 to 2025. HRV was the most frequently detected virus (796 cases, 30.7%), followed by ADV (692, 26.6%), RSV (536, 20.6%), HBoV (313, 12.1%), IFV (155, 6.0%) and HMPV (105, 4.0%) (Figure 2A; Table 1). Pathogen–climate associations were estimated using a quasi-Poisson model that adjusted for seasonality, secular trend, and lagged meteorological exposures.ResultsAmong 2,597 virus-positive cases, the leading pathogens were HRV (30.7%), ADV (26.6%), and RSV (20.6%), followed by HBoV (12.1%), IFV (6.0%), and HMPV (4.0%). RSV and HBoV were most prevalent in infants and toddlers, in line with airway and immune development (Feng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022); ADV peaked in school-aged children and IFV in the older preschool-to-school-age range, consistent with close-contact transmission in schools and other crowded settings (Fang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023); and HMPV showed an intermediate distribution. To our knowledge, the dataset is unusual for northern China in spanning six respiratory viruses, including the comparatively under-surveyed HRV, HBoV and HMPV, over the full 2023–2025 post-pandemic rebound window, with a complete and time-matched monthly meteorological record.4.1Principal epidemiological featuresAcross the six viruses, HRV, ADV and RSV were the leading causes of pediatric LRTI, and each pathogen carried a well-defined demographic profile. The strong age-group × pathogen association reinforces the need for an explicitly age-stratified surveillance framework.The six pathogens also fell into two distinct seasonal groups.
